paragraphs.text: March 31. The Life of Saint John the Bishop, the Silent, of the monastery of our father Sabbas. First I will present an account of Father John the Silent, who lived in the monastery of the blessed Sabbas, since he surpassed all the others both in years and in the splendor of his life. This holy father of ours, John, was from Nicopolis in Armenia, born to parents named Encratius and Euphemia, who abounded in wealth and ancestral distinction and had distinguished themselves in many high civic offices, in military commands, and in leadership of the people. The Byzantine and Armenian [?] provide many accounts of them and their achievements. I wish to pass these over, so as not to overwhelm the reader at the very beginning of the account, relating only those things about him that will plainly make him known to everyone. He was

born, then, as he himself told me, on the eighth day of the month of January, in the fourth year of the reign of Marcian, beloved of God. Since both his parents were Christians, he was brought up as a Christian together with his siblings. After some time had passed, and his parents had died in Christ and their property had been divided, this God-bearing father gave himself to God as his portion and built a church in that city to the most-praised Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary. He renounced worldly concerns in the eighteenth year of his life. Taking in ten brothers who desired salvation, he established a monastery there. Throughout all the years of his youth, he took great care to restrain his appetite and despise pride, knowing that a full belly knows neither how to keep vigil nor how to remain chaste, and that pride cannot endure silence, while self-control cannot be achieved without vigilance, purity, and humility. Thus he labored in his youth, keeping his mind free from distraction and his speech blameless, seasoned with divine salt. Through fruitful words and deeds he trained them in a life of self-control, not

allowing them to remain either overburdened or untested, but, leading them little by little and nourishing them with divine drink, to bear fruit worthy of their calling was what he urged them to do. When he reached his twenty-eighth year, And as the grace that rested upon him shone forth and spread everywhere, the metropolitan of Sebaste, persuaded by the reports about him and by the people of the city of Colonia, who entreated him, summoned him as though on some other business, and, after he had passed through the ranks of the clergy in order, appointed him bishop, since the bishop of that city had died. And so, having accepted the episcopate against his will, he did not change the rule of his monastic life. Instead, as bishop he labored as though he were in a monastery, devoting himself especially to silence. He was ashamed not only to be seen naked by another, but even to see himself naked, reflecting on Adam’s nakedness and what concerned it. He considered not washing to be one of the great virtues. To put it simply, he made every effort in every way to please God, through fasting and prayers and bodily purification, and, in purity of heart, always cleansing his thoughts and every lofty thing rising against the knowledge

of God. His brother Pergamius, too, having found favor with both emperors and having held many high civic offices, was enlightened by this man’s virtue and made great efforts to please God. His nephew Theodore, too, the distinguished comptroller, received instruction from this godly man, who had grown old in virtue, and, enlightening his soul through what he heard, greatly pleased God, together with his whole household. This Theodore is now admired by the entire council of nobles and by our devout emperor Justinian for his wisdom, purity of life, right faith, and mercy. But this belongs to a later time; I return to the chronological order. When this godly John had spent nine years as bishop, it happened that the husband of his sister Mary, named Pasinicus, was governing Armenia. At Satan’s prompting, he began to oppress and trouble the church entrusted to John, not allowing those who administered it to do what was proper in providing for and arranging the church’s needs, and forcibly dragging away those who sought refuge under its laws, and overturning what had been established by law. Though he was often entreated and admonished with the words of God,

he grew worse, Mary, John’s sister, having already died. From that time, then, the righteous man fell into bitter sorrow. He was compelled to go to Constantinople. After staying there and doing what was beneficial for his church, at the end of Zeno’s reign, when Euphemius, archbishop of Constantinople, had exerted himself on his behalf, the man pleasing to God resolved to go to the Holy City and, freed from the cares of this world, to live in silence. Having dismissed the clergy who were with him with the instructions he had given, and having concealed himself from everyone, he found himself alone, boarded a ship, and came to Jerusalem. He stayed in a guesthouse outside the city, which had been built by the blessed Eudocia. In this guesthouse there is a church of Saint George the martyr. While staying there, he saw the worldly bustle and became troubled in his mind. With tears he prayed to God to be led to a quiet place pleasing to God and suited to salvation. While he was thus staying in the guesthouse and praying to God about this, he was walking alone at night in the courtyard and, looking up into heaven, suddenly saw a star shaped like a cross coming toward him. He heard a voice speaking from that light: “If you wish to be saved,

then follow this light.” Believing, he went out quickly and followed that light. The light led him and brought him to the Great Lavra of our holy father Sabas. At that time Sallustius was patriarch in Jerusalem. Having arrived at the Great Lavra, he found the blessed Sabas, who had gathered a community of 108 monks. They lived in great material poverty, but were rich in spiritual gifts. The blessed Sabas received him and entrusted him to the monastery’s steward, to assign him service as one of the newcomers, for they did not know the treasure of goodness within him. Let no one be surprised that the treasure of John’s virtuous deeds was hidden from the venerable elder Sabas. Rather, let such a person consider that when God wishes to reveal something to his saints, they are prophets; but when he wishes to conceal it, they see like everyone else. The prophet Elisha bears witness to my words when he speaks about the Shunammite woman. “For her soul is in anguish, and the Lord has hidden it from me.” But the godly John was carrying out every task of obedience, serving the steward and the other fathers with all diligence

and humility, bringing water up from the stream and cooking for the workmen, and working for them with stone and at the other building tasks, while the monastery’s guesthouse was being built. Afterward, the blessed Sabas appointed him as cook, to cook and serve the whole brotherhood. Accepting this service eagerly and joyfully, he served all the fathers, attending to each one with complete humility and gentleness. While he was performing this service, a monastery began to be built north of the lavra, to receive there those newly arriving from the world, so that the truth of monastic life might first be learned there, and only then would they live in the lavra, after learning the monastic rule thoroughly, as the blessed Sabas declared, saying: “Just as the flower comes before the fruit, so life in a monastery comes before life in solitude.” While this monastery was being built, that righteous man was required to undertake another service: besides cooking, he had to carry food to the workmen, ten stadia away from the monastery. When a year had passed in such

service, and all the fathers had been edified by his conduct, his purity, and his spiritual understanding, our father Sabas gave him a cell for a life of silence. The venerable John received the cell and, having been instructed to live in silence, remained there for three years, neither appearing before anyone at all nor tasting anything for five days each week. On Saturday and Sunday, he entered the church before everyone else and left last, after everyone else, standing fervently and with fear and complete reverence during the chanting, according to what is said in the Psalms: “Serve God with fear, and rejoice before him with trembling.” So great was his compunction that he wept profusely at the time of the sorrowless sacrifice and could not restrain himself, so that the fathers who saw his gift of tears marveled at God, the giver of good things. When the three years had ended, the administration of the monastery was entrusted to him. And God helped him in everything. The monastery was blessed, and the brotherhood grew under his administration. When he had completed his service, blessed Sabbas wished to appoint him to an ecclesiastical rank, since he was a good and accomplished monk. Taking him to the Holy City,

he brought him to blessed Archbishop Elias and, describing his virtues, asked him to ordain him a priest. When the archbishop heard about him, he went to the holy Place of the Skull, wishing to ordain him with his own hands. But this great father, finding himself detained, so that he could not escape under the circumstances, said to the archbishop, “Honored father, since I have sinned, I ask to tell you two blessed men something privately. And if you both judge me worthy, then I will accept ordination.” Taking him aside onto the ascent to holy Golgotha, he said, “Spare my life, I beg Your Holiness, and reveal this secret to no one, lest I leave this place too.” When the archbishop had assured him of this, he said to him, “Father, I have been ordained bishop of a certain city. But because my transgressions multiplied, I fled far away and settled in the desert, awaiting God’s visitation. I thought it right, while I still have bodily strength, to serve and work for the fathers, so that when I grow weak, I may receive the service of others without condemnation.” Hearing this, the archbishop marveled. He summoned blessed Sabbas and said to him, “He has told me something, and it is not possible to ordain him

a priest. But from this day onward, let him live in quiet, with no one troubling him.” Having said this, the archbishop dismissed them. But blessed Sabbas, troubled in his mind, went thirty stadia away from the monastery and entered a cave. Falling down before God, he prayed with tears, saying, “Why, Lord, have you disregarded me so completely as to let me be deceived and think John worthy of the priesthood? And now, Master and Lord, reveal the truth about him to me, for my soul is sorrowful to the point of death, if the vessel that I thought sanctified and useful, and worthy of receiving your divine chrism, has proved useless before your majesty.” As Father Sabbas, with tears, [?] these and similar words, An angelic voice came, saying, “John is not an unworthy vessel, but a chosen one. For, having already been ordained a bishop, he cannot now become a priest.” Thus far the vision. But Father Sabbas, being accustomed to appearances of God and visions of angels, was not afraid, but rejoiced. He came to the cell of the venerable John, embraced him, and said, “Father John, you concealed from me the gift bestowed on you, but my Lord revealed it.” The godly John

said, “I am distressed, Father, for I did not want anyone to learn this secret. And now I will not be able to live in this place.” But the elder Sabbas pledged his word before God to tell no one at all about this. From then on, John began to keep silence in his cell, neither coming to church nor speaking to anyone at all except the one who served him, for four years. The only exception was on the day of the consecration of the venerable church in the monastery, dedicated to the Most Holy Mother of God and Ever-Virgin Mary. For only then, after Archbishop Elias had been entreated by our holy father Sabbas, and much effort had been made, having come for the consecration, he compelled John to come and greet him. The patriarch, after speaking with him and coming to love his spiritual understanding, his disposition, and his pleasant conversation, held him in honor throughout all the years of his patriarchate. When four years had passed, and the blessed Sabbas had departed from the lavra for the region of Scythopolis because of the misconduct of the newcomers who were in the New Lavra, the venerable John, fleeing that disorderly company, went away into the wilderness of Ruba in the fiftieth year of his life. He kept silence there for six years, separating himself entirely from human society,

loving to speak to God in silence and cleansing the vision of his mind through long endurance, so as to behold the Lord’s glory with unveiled face, making every effort to advance from glory to glory, with a longing for greater things. Every two or three days, making allowance for the body’s natural needs, he would come out of the cave and go about the wilderness to gather wild-growing melagria [?], on which those who withdraw into the wilderness feed. And on one of those days, at the beginning of that godly way of life, when he was not yet familiar with that wilderness, he went out to gather. And he lost his way and wandered onto trackless slopes, and could not find a way back to the cave. Unable to go on, he collapsed, gasping for breath. And there, suddenly, through divine intervention, he was lifted into the air. Like the prophet Habakkuk, as I believe, he found himself in his own cave. As the year was coming to an end, having become familiar with that wilderness and identified the place from which he had been carried through the air, he found it to be five miles from the cave. A certain brother came to Rouba and stayed with him for a short time, living a hermit's life with him.

Having had more than enough of such hardship, this brother said to the elder: "Now that Easter is approaching, let us go up to the monastery, father, and celebrate Easter and the feast days with the fathers, since we have no food here except these melagria [?]." But the godly John did not want to go there, since our father Sabas was not there, but had left the monastery, as we have said. He tried to persuade the distressed brother, who wanted to leave, saying: "Let us remain in silence, brother, and believe that he who fed six hundred thousand in the wilderness for forty years will also feed us, providing not merely what we need, but an abundance. For he said this: 'I will not neglect you, nor will I abandon you.' And in the Gospel he said: 'Do not worry, saying, "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we drink?" or "What shall we wear?" For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. Only seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and these things will be added to you.' So be patient, my child, and prefer the narrow way to the broad one. For living without restraint here brings eternal torment, while suffering here prepares an abundance of good things." Although the father spoke these and similar words,

the brother did not listen, but departed along the road leading to the monastery. After he had left, a certain unknown man came directly to the elder, bringing a donkey laden with many good things. He had [?] fine, warm loaves, wine, and olive oil, fresh cheeses, eggs, and a jar of honey. He unloaded them and went away. And our venerable father John rejoiced in spirit at God's visitation. But the brother who had gone away lost his way and suffered greatly. He returned on the third day, dying of hunger and exhausted, having had his fill of the fruit of his disobedience. Finding so many good things in the cave, he repented of his unbelief and disobedience and fell at the elder’s feet in shame, asking to receive forgiveness. Taking thought for human weakness and feeling compassion for the brother, the elder raised him up and comforted him, saying, “Know for certain that the Lord can prepare a table in the wilderness.” Now in that year Al-Mundhir Sisik, having assumed royal rank over those who paid tribute to the Persians, marched against Arabia and Palestine in great rage against the Greeks, plundering everywhere and taking captives by surprise, and committing many lawless

deeds after the capture of Amida. When a large force of soldiers had scattered throughout this desert, and the leaders and guardians of that desert had warned the monasteries of the Great Lavra to be on their guard against the soldiers, the fathers told this honored father not to go into [?], but to come to the lavra and remain in his own cell. But the godly John, having tasted divine sweetness through silence, lovingly clung to it and could not withdraw. Reflecting within himself, he said, “If God does not care for me, why am I even alive?” And so, having made the Most High his refuge, he remained without fear. But God, who always spares his servants, commanded his angels, as it is written, to protect the holy man. Wishing to reassure him when he had become a little afraid, he sent as a visible guard a very large and fearsome lion, which guarded him night and day from the plots of murderous pagans. Yet on the first night, when he saw the lion sleeping, he was a little afraid, as he himself told me. But when it followed him night and day without leaving him, and he saw the lion driving the soldiers away [?], he offered up thankful

songs to God, who does not leave the rod of sinners over the portion of the righteous. Now our blessed father Sabas, having come from Scythopolis and established the New Lavra, came to the settlement of caves and remembered the vision he had once had concerning the holy John. He went to him in Ruba and said to him, “See, God has kept you safe from the enemy’s attack and made this known to you by sending you a visible guardian. Now rise, do your human part, and flee as the fathers did.” Then he led him into the great lavra and shut him in a cell. He was fifty-five years old. No one else in the community knew that he was a bishop. When many years had passed, God arranged to reveal John’s hidden treasure in the following way. A certain man from the land of Asia, named Etherius, had been honored with the rank of bishop and lived worthily of it. He came to Jerusalem and venerated the holy places and the life-giving wood of the cross. He distributed much of his wealth to the poor and to the monasteries. Then he left the holy city to return to his homeland and boarded

a ship. After sailing a short distance out to sea, he encountered a contrary wind and returned to Ashkelon with great difficulty. When he intended to sail again after two days, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “You cannot leave unless you return to the holy city and go to the lavra of the monk Sabbas and speak with the monk John the Silent, a righteous man who leads a good life, who is a bishop and once possessed worldly wealth, but who, out of fear and love of God, has scorned everything worldly and through voluntary poverty and abstinence has disciplined himself.” Then Etherius awoke from sleep, considered the vision, and, making inquiries with all diligence, came to the lavra of Father Sabbas. He told the fathers about the vision and was led to the silent monk. He greeted him and stayed with him for two days. As their conversation continued, he put him under oath to tell him about himself and reveal who he was. Thus compelled, he told him about his family, his homeland, and his episcopal office. When Etherius learned this, he was greatly amazed and said, “Truly, even now holy stones are rolling

about on the ground.” Then he bowed before the righteous man and went to the blessed Sabbas. He told him and all the fathers about the godly John. From that time onward, John’s origins and his episcopal rank were known. In the seventy-ninth year of this John’s life, our holy father Sabas fell asleep in peace, on the fifth day of December. Then this precious pearl was grieved in his mind, because he had not left his cell and come to be present at the holy father’s death. While he was in such great sorrow, weeping with tears over the loss of his father, our father appeared to him in a dream, saying: “Do not be troubled, Father John. For although I have been separated from you in the flesh, I am with you in spirit.” When John said, “Pray to the Master that he may receive me too,” blessed Sabas said, “That cannot happen now, for a great trial is about to come upon the lavra, and God wishes you to remain in the flesh to encourage and strengthen those who struggle for the faith and those who toil.” Having seen and heard this, godly John rejoiced, shaking off his grief over his father. He was troubled only about the trial that had been foretold.

Then the thought came to him to see how the soul is separated from the body. While he was praying to God about this, he was carried away in his mind to holy Bethlehem. In the porch of that venerable church, he saw a wondrous, holy man lying at the point of death, and his soul being received by angels and carried up to heaven with a certain divine song of praise and a sweet fragrance. He wished to see with his own eyes whether this was so, and he rose that very hour and went to holy Bethlehem. He found that the man had given up his soul at that very hour. He kissed his venerable body in that porch, wrapped it, and laid him in the burial places of the holy men. Then he returned to his cell. Two disciples of this enlightened elder, Theodore and John, told me, saying, “After holy Sabas fell asleep, the elder sent us on an errand to Livias. On the way, after we had crossed the Jordan, some people met us and said, ‘Be careful, for there is a lion ahead of you.’ But we thought, ‘God is able to protect us through the prayers of our father. For did we go out of our own accord? Rather, we are carrying out the elder’s command.’ With this thought, we went on.

And there was a lion coming toward us. We were terribly afraid, and no strength remained in us. And soon we both saw the elder between us, taking away our fear and telling us to [?]. Then the lion fled from us as though wounded. And we both went unharmed and came to the elder. He spoke first, saying to us, “Did you see how I was with you in your distress?” “Yet even here I prayed earnestly to God for you both, and behold, he has shown you mercy.” One of his disciples, named Theodore, also told me this: “For many years he took only broth, and he mixed it with ashes from the incense burner and ate it that way. I caught him doing this in the following way. Once he forgot to bolt the door, and I wanted to give him some hot water. I touched the door, and it opened, and I found him emptying the incense burner into his bowl. He was deeply distressed at this. Wishing to dispel his distress, I said to the elder, ‘You are not the only one who does this, Father. Many others in this lavra do so too, fulfilling the Scripture that says, “I ate ashes like bread.”’ And only with difficulty did I manage to change the elder’s mood with these words.” A certain woman, Cappadocian by birth and named Basilina, who was a deaconess, came to Jerusalem, bringing with her a nephew who held the rank of [?].

He was otherwise self-controlled, but he was not in communion with the most revered Church, having accepted the false faith of Severus. The deaconess made great efforts to change his faith and bring him into the most revered Church. She also asked every righteous man to pray for him. Having heard of the grace bestowed on this godly John, the woman wished to bow before him. But learning that a woman could not enter the monastery, she summoned Theodore, his disciple, and asked him to take her nephew and bring him to the holy elder, believing that through his prayers God would change her nephew’s hardness of heart, and he would be found worthy to enter into communion with the most revered Church. The disciple Theodore took him and went down to the elder, and knocked on the door as usual. As the elder was about to open it, they bowed to one another, and the disciple said, “Bless us, Father.” The elder opened the door and said to the disciple, “You, indeed, I bless.” But that man has no blessing. The disciple said, “Not so, Father.” The elder answered, “Truly, I will not bless him until he abandons the beliefs of those who have separated themselves and professes communion with the universal Church.” Hearing this,

the man marveled at the elder’s gift of spiritual insight. And, changed by this wonder, he promised with firm conviction to enter into communion with the universal Church. Then the elder blessed him, raised him up, and first gave him Communion in the most pure Mysteries, having removed all wavering from his heart. When Basilina heard this, she grew in love even more, so that she wished to see the elder with her own eyes. She thought of dressing as a man and going to him in the lavra to tell him about herself. When this had been disclosed to him through an angelic revelation, he sent word to her, saying, “Know that if you come, you will not see me. So do not trouble yourself, but rather be patient. Wherever you may be, I will come to you in a dream and hear about your circumstances. And whatever God puts into my mind, I will tell you.” Hearing this and believing, she received a clear vision. For he appeared to her in a dream, saying, “See, God has sent me to you. Tell me what you want.” After telling him about herself, she received a fitting answer and arose, giving thanks to God and to the holy man. And when the elder’s disciple came, she described the father’s appearance and face. I heard this from the deaconess Basilina herself. The place where the holy elder had shut himself away

has a very high cliff to the west, [?] of the place where the roof of his cell is fastened. The rock of the cliff is so very dry and free of moisture that it produces no dampness at all in the cell. One day, the holy elder took the seed of a single fig and said to his two disciples, Theodore and John, “Listen to me, my children. If God’s love for humanity gives this seed and this rock the power to produce fruit, then know that God is freely giving me the kingdom of heaven.” Having said this, he fastened the fig to the crumbling rock. And God, who had commanded Aaron’s rod, though it was dry, to grow and blossom, also commanded the solid, dry rock to bring forth growth, as a demonstration through miracles. and what grace his servant received afterward. When the elder saw the shoot, he thanked God with tears. The shoot gradually grew upward until it reached the roof, which he then removed. And, to put it simply, that year it bore three figs. The elder took them and kissed them with tears, and ate them. He thanked God, who had given him assurance, and gave a little to each of his two disciples. And this tree cries out, bearing witness to the elder’s goodness. From the time the God-bearing elder ate the figs, he was preparing himself. Since he had reached extreme old age,

the disciples opened [?] to serve him. When I went in to him and saw the awe-inspiring miracle of the tree, I examined carefully how it had taken root and whether the rock had a crack, but I could find none. In my amazement I said, “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how untraceable his ways!” For those who have had long experience of the lavra of blessed Sabas know, I think, that neither a fig tree nor any other tree can grow in the enclosure, because of the great heat and dryness of the air at the lavra. But if anyone has in mind the trees of the small monastery beside the road, let him know that this came about through the prayers of blessed Sabas. They found deep soil and a slope at the foot of the mountain down which rainwater flowed. For this reason, when many of us began planting beside the stream, where the soil was also deep, and we watered throughout the winter, the plantings scarcely managed to take root over the course of a year, because of the great [?] and the intense heat, as I have said. And so, having gathered a little out of much, I committed it to writing, leaving untold his labors for the faith, which he displayed against Origen and Theodore of Mopsuestia, and the ordinances and defenders, and the persecutions he suffered, according to the gospel,

for the apostolic ordinances. But I will leave these things for other writers to recount, for he saw clearly that after his death many would be more eager to sow discord. But the labors, persecutions, and hardships he endured for the orthodox faith, and his victories and glorious life—in every respect, so to speak, during our lifetime— and the virtues that shone in him made him renowned, as I heard his holy tongue say: He was ordained bishop in the twenty-eighth year of his age, as we have already related above. And he spent ten years as bishop, and at first lived in the monastery for twelve years. From these, subtract six years. And shut away in a cell, in which he remains in silence to this day, he completed forty-seven years in God. And now he has reached the hundred and fourth year of his life. And he is very old, radiant in face and [?] in soul, and filled with divine grace. Let us poor people also pray that God may make him stronger and stronger and bring his course to its end in peace. For to him belong glory, honor, power, and worship—to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
